newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. blames EU for WTO farm statement hitch.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blames EU for WTO farm statement hitch.

text.p: Negotiations over a statement on farm trade to be issued at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting had been stalled by the European Union, a senior U.S. official said in Hong Kong on Friday.

"Some countries, especially the European Union, are concerned that some exporting countries want to move a little faster than they (EU) are prepared to move," August Schumacher, administrator with the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Foreign Agriculture Service, told reporters here.

Philippine Trade and Industry Secretary Cesar Bautista told reporters at the WTO meeting in Singapore earlier on Friday that wrangling between the EU on one hand and the U.S. and the Cairns Group, linking farm exporting nations from Australia to Uruguay, on the other was only settled after the dropping of a paragraph mandating preliminary studies on farm issues in 1997.

The Cairns Group will now issue a statement separate from the main WTO agricultural working committee's text attacking what it regards as gross violations of trading agreements in the EU's support for farm subsidies, Bautista said.

The closing declaration of the WTO's Singapore ministerial meeting said: "Progress has been made also in advancing the WTO reform programme in agriculture, including in implementation of agreed market access concessions and domestic subsidy and export subsidy commitments."

The declaration said the trade ministers had taken note of concerns over the "possible negative effects of the agricultural reform programme on least-developed and net food-importing developing countries".
Schumacher said: "There are active discussions on agriculture in terms of preparatory work that needs to be done in 1997, leading to negotiations in 1999.
"I have every faith there will be no going back during analytical preparatory work," he said.
Schumacher said the United States wanted to move into preparatory work for negotiations scheduled to begin next year.

A senior U.S. government source said: "We want a lot of the countries to present their data so it can be analysed well ahead of time. A lot of countries have made mistakes in the past and now they want to get out of their commitments -- and we say no.
"Europe doesn't want that, because they are fearful the U.S. will be too well prepared." he said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
